subject: Accounting
title: Understanding Equity
description: A micro-lesson that makes Understanding Equity usable.

hook.text: Sell everything, pay all debts. What's left belongs to the owners. That's equity.

buildup.text: Equity represents owners' claims on the business after all liabilities are settled.

discovery.text: It grows when the company earns profit and shrinks when it pays dividends or takes losses.

twist.text: A company can have massive assets but tiny equity if it's loaded with debt.

climax.text: Investors watch equity closely—it reveals how much truly belongs to shareholders.

punchline.text: Equity is the owners' real stake in the game.

quiz.question: When does equity typically increase?
options: When it takes on more debt

details.summary: Equity represents the owners' residual interest in a company's assets after deducting all liabilities. It's what the owners truly 'own' and reflects both their direct investments and the company's accumulated earnings that haven't been distributed.
details.whyItMatters: Equity is the measure of ownership value. It tells investors how much of the company's assets would belong to shareholders if all debts were paid. Changes in equity reveal whether value is being created or destroyed.
takeaways: Equity equals assets minus liabilities—the residual claim after creditors are paid
Equity increases through owner investments and net income; decreases through distributions and net losses
Book equity on the balance sheet often differs significantly from market capitalization

faq.question: What is the difference between book equity and market equity?
faq.answer: Think of equity as what remains after debts are paid. If your home is worth $400,000 and you owe $250,000 on the mortgage, your equity is $150,000. In a company, equity represents the shareholders’ residual claim on assets after all liabilities are settled.

faq.question: How does net income affect equity?
faq.answer: Net income increases retained earnings, which is a component of equity. When a company earns profit, its assets increase (more cash or receivables) while liabilities stay the same, so equity must increase to keep the accounting equation balanced.
